processing: Both are made exactly like any Longjing: a short wither, then pan-fired and pressed flat in the wok in two passes until dry. The difference is entirely in the plant.
harvest_season: Spring only. Longjing 43 buds early and is usually picked from mid to late March; Qunti bushes wake up a week or more later, so pre-Qingming Qunti is scarcer.
appearance_dry: Longjing 43: uniform, bright green, flat blades; Qunti: mixed sizes, yellow-green to 'brown rice' colour, slightly less polished.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green and clear in both; Qunti tends a shade more golden.
appearance_wet: 43 opens into neat, near-identical bud-and-one-leaf sets; Qunti leaves vary in size and shade.
taste_profile: 43 is clean and tidy, toasted bean with a brisk edge; Qunti has the richer aroma and flavour, rounder and more savoury, with a longer, sweeter finish.

brewing.notes: Taste them side by side in identical glasses with the same water; the cultivar difference shows most clearly in the second steep and in the finish.

vintage_note: Both are sold only as the current spring's harvest. Longjing 43 is the first Dragon Well of the year, typically from mid to late March, and dominates pre-Qingming lots; Qunti comes in roughly a week later and sells at a premium when it genuinely comes from the West Lake villages. Neither is meant to be aged: drink within the year, keep it cold and sealed.
description:
Ask a Hangzhou tea seller what is in the bag and you will hear one of two answers: Longjing 43 or Qunti. They are the two cultivars behind almost all genuine Dragon Well, and the difference is bigger than most drinkers expect, so it deserves a separate look.

Qunti zhong ('population variety') is the old seed-grown landrace: every bush is genetically a little different, they bud late and unevenly, and the finished leaf is a jumble of sizes with a yellowish, brown-rice tone. Longjing 43 is a single clone selected from that population by the tea research institute in Hangzhou and released as a national cultivar in the 1980s. It buds early, every shoot looks the same, the leaf fires up a prettier bright green, and it yields more. That is why it took over most of the gardens.

In the cup, 43 is the cleaner, tidier tea: toasted bean, brisk and pretty, sometimes a little thin. Qunti has the richer aroma and flavour, with more body, a longer sweet and savoury finish, and more variation from steep to steep. Plenty of old-school drinkers pay extra for Qunti from the Shifeng and Longjing village slopes; plenty of others honestly prefer the clean, brisk cup of 43. Brew them side by side at 80 °C in two glasses and you will have an opinion within ten minutes.

Buying notes: because 43 is early, the first 'mingqian' Longjing every year is 43; pre-Qingming Qunti exists but there is far less of it and it costs more. Other early clones such as Wuniuzao and Zhongcha 108 are legitimately used for inexpensive Zhejiang Longjing, but they are sometimes dressed up as West Lake tea; the tell is a very early picking date and an unnaturally uniform, bright-green leaf. An honest seller will name the cultivar without being asked twice.
history:
Qunti is the older of the two: the traditional population of Longjing bushes, described in Hangzhou reporting as native to the Shifeng area. Every bush differs a little.

Longjing 43 came out of that population. The Tea Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences picked a single plant in 1960, numbered it 6043, and saw it recognised as a national cultivar in 1987. Unlike Qunti it is propagated from cuttings.

The practical difference is the calendar. Longjing 43 buds in mid to late March and is picked about 7 to 10 days ahead of Qunti, and that head start is a large part of why it spread. In 2023 and 2026 the West Lake area announced separate opening dates for the two, with 43 going first and Qunti following in late March.
